title: Jake Bauers, fresh off a dream season, agrees to 4-year deal with Red Sox: Source
author: Will Sammon
content:
Free-agent first baseman Jake Bauers is not striking it rich with the New York Yankees after all, as Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy famously suggested after the final out of the World Series: Bauers is headed to Boston instead.

Bauers is joining the Red Sox on a four-year, $58 million contract, according to a league source who was granted anonymity because he was not authorized to speak publicly about the deal.

Last month, Bauers, 31, was named NLCS MVP after driving in six runs in a sweep of the two-time defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers. In Game 3 of that series, Bauers punctuated an 11-pitch at-bat against left-hander Blake Snell by smashing a two-run, go-ahead homer.

After squeezing the last out of the Brewers’ first World Series title, Bauers handed the ball to Murphy, whose hot-mic comment to Bauers as they hugged soon spread throughout the baseball world: “You’re going to be a rich f—er,” Murphy said. “Just remember when you’re on that horses— Yankees team and you guys are all playing for yourself? Just remember, say, ‘This is the way we used to do it.’”

For Bauers, the championship and the lucrative contract that followed represent the pinnacle of an arduous journey in pro ball. After the 2024 season, the Brewers removed Bauers from their 40-man roster. His career OPS in the big leagues was .662, 19 percent worse than league average. His career bWAR total: -1.9. He elected to become a free agent rather than accept a minor-league assignment. At 29, he had already cycled through seven organizations, getting traded four times and designated for assignment once.

Bauers said that he had planned to retire. He daydreamed about moving across the globe and leaving baseball behind.

“I was pretty dead-set (on retiring),” Bauers told The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal in October. “You go through enough in this game, and that thought pops up in your head more than one time. It could have changed as the offseason went on. But in that moment, I was dead-set on it.”

With his wife, Lauren, expecting the couple’s second child, Bauers tabled retirement talk and re-signed with the Brewers on a minor-league contract in January 2025. He took a step forward that season, posting a .752 OPS in a platoon role. He fully broke out in 2026, slashing .266/.389.484 (.874 OPS), and then starring in the postseason. Now, he is an important piece of the Red Sox’s plans.

For Boston, more moves are coming. Bauers adds another power element to the middle of the Red Sox order, serving as a left-handed complement at first base to Willson Contreras, Boston’s best hitter last season.

Bauers is a subpar defensive first baseman, and though he has experience at both corner outfield spots, he’s not great defensively there, either. A team source, granted anonymity because he wasn’t authorized to speak publicly, noted the plan is for Bauers to split time at designated hitter and first base with Contreras.

Coming off the best offensive season of his career, Bauers’ 26 homers were just one fewer than Contreras’ Red Sox-leading 27 homers in 2026.

Still, Bauers addition continues to crowd an already jam-packed roster. First baseman Triston Casas, who just started a winter ball assignment in the Dominican Republic, is likely to remain in Triple-A Worcester as he continues to rehab from a series of injuries over the last two years.

If the Red Sox plan to use Bauers at designated hitter, they will have to address the surplus at first base and DH. Masataka Yoshida has served as DH the last two years when healthy, while Roman Anthony has split time between the outfield and DH. Meanwhile, the Red Sox have four other outfielders on the 40-man roster: Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela and utility outfielder Eli White.

Moving Yoshida may be difficult, given he is owed $18.6 million in the final year of a five-year deal. Duran has been in trade rumors in recent years and is owed roughly $11 million in arbitration next season. Coming off a career-worst season, though, he may be hard to move, but the Red Sox will have to cut ties somewhere to make room on the roster.

Regardless, the Red Sox are adding a potent bat in Bauers to their lineup, which finished 23rd in MLB in runs scored in 2026. Bauers, a lefty bat, showed this season that he can handle both right-handed and left-handed pitchers (.863 OPS vs. RHPs, .901 OPS vs. LHPs). His powerful production in 2026 turned heads. Before this season, Bauers had averaged about 10 home runs per season as a part-time player from 2018-25. But the underlying data suggests Bauer’s breakout is real; according to Baseball Savant, he finished in the top 10 percent of the league in barrel rate, hard-hit rate, bat speed and average exit velocity.

Two years ago, Bauers contemplated retiring.

Now, it will be a while before he hangs them up.
